activity.notes: Anizham Thirunal Marthanda Varma (c.1706–1758) succeeded Rama Varma in 1729 as ruler of Venad/Travancore, consolidated and expanded that existing southern Kerala kingship, and died in 1758. This Activity is his documented 1729–1758 royal reign, NOT an assertion that an entirely new sovereign state was created ex nihilo in 1729. Venad is the earlier name/nucleus of Travancore, and any distinct live ATLAS Venad and/or Travancore identities must undergo source- and UUID-backed continuity review rather than automatic duplicate creation, false merge, or speculative reassignment. His army defeated Dutch East India Company forces at Colachel in 1741, and his dedication of the kingdom to Padmanabha in 1750 was a sacral state-form/royal-policy event, not a second reign. Year granularity only; do not infer precise accession day. Distinguish the later Uthram Thirunal Marthanda Varma (r. 1846–1860).

sources.title: Government of Kerala, Directorate of Industries and Commerce — Industrial Profile (Thiruvananthapuram)
sources.citation_text: Kerala state government history explicitly dates Marthanda Varma's rule to 1729–1758 and relates his consolidation of Travancore.

sources.title: Government of Kerala, Revenue Department — Kumbalam Village Office historical account
sources.citation_text: Official Kerala revenue history explicitly identifies Anizham Thirunal Marthanda Varma as Maharaja of Travancore (1729–58), records the 1755 Karappuram annexation and clarifies separate neighboring Cochin sovereignty.

sources.title: Kerala Tourism — Krishnapuram Palace, Kayamkulam
sources.citation_text: State tourism authority dates King Anizham Thirunal Marthanda Varma to 1729–1758 and confirms his annexation of Kayamkulam into Travancore.

sources.title: Indiana University Press — Deep Cosmopolitanism, Ch. 4: Kings, Sultans, and Colonialists
sources.citation_text: Academic historical synthesis says the rising Kingdom of Travancore had previously been known as Venad, and marks Marthanda Varma's 1729 accession as the turning point toward centralized state power.
